summary: This program builds two sets of song titles \\u2014 yours and a friend's \\u2014 and then uses the Set operations retainAll, addAll, and removeAll to work out which songs you share, what a combined playlist would look like, and which songs are yours alone.

lines.text: The imports at the top carry over from the earlier steps of this playlist app, and one is missing here: because the code creates HashSet objects, add `import java.util.HashSet;` to this list or the file will not compile.

The variable is declared as the Set interface but built as a HashSet, which is the usual Java habit of coding to the general type and choosing the implementation on the right. A Set refuses duplicates, so adding "Respect" a second time would silently change nothing.

Passing a set into the HashSet constructor makes a working copy of your playlist. Each of the three operations below modifies its copy in place, so myTitles and friendTitles are never damaged and can be compared again.
retainAll throws away every element that is not also in the friend's playlist, leaving only the songs the two of you have in common.

removeAll strips out the friend's songs, leaving the ones only you have. The direction matters: starting from friendTitles and removing myTitles would instead give you the songs of theirs you have not heard.
A HashSet makes no promise about order, so the titles may print in an order that looks random and can differ between runs. Use a TreeSet if you want the results in alphabetical order.
